one_liner: Zig word-frequency count with zero-copy slice keys in a StringHashMap; 1.74x faster than every C/C++ build in LangArena Etc::Words.
what_it_does: A LangArena benchmark task, not a library: split a 325,090-byte string of 50,000 generated lowercase words (3 to 8 letters, single spaces) on ' ', count each word in a hash map, then fold the top word's count, its djb2 hash and the vocabulary size into a checksum. The Zig code is Words.runImpl in zig/src/words.zig (about 130 lines): a fresh std.heap.ArenaAllocator per iteration, a std.StringHashMap(u32) on that arena, std.mem.splitScalar over the text with getOrPut per token, then a linear scan of the map for the maximum. To use it you write Zig; nothing links into a C++ program.
how_it_is_fast: Allocation and container choice, not code generation. splitScalar yields slices into the original text and getOrPut stores those slices as the keys, so no word is copied or individually allocated; std.StringHashMap is an open-addressing table (Wyhash with seed 0, mem.eql compare, power-of-two capacity, 80% max load, one metadata byte per slot) whose storage comes from the arena and is released by one arena.deinit. The C++ baseline copies the 325 KB text into a std::istringstream every iteration, extracts each token with operator>> into a std::string and try_emplaces it into a node-based std::unordered_map<std::string,int>, which allocates a node holding its own key copy for each of the 18,623 distinct words per iteration; the C version strdup()s the whole text, tokenizes with strtok_r and mallocs an entry plus a strdup'd key per distinct word in uthash. The ReleaseFast build of the same source (Zig/Unchecked) runs 0.57 s, so safety checks and other ReleaseSafe differences take about 37% of the 0.91 s production time.
when_to_use: Batch word or token counting in Zig over in-memory ASCII text that outlives the map, so the keys can stay slices into the text.
Build-read-drop maps: one count per batch, read once, then freed in a single arena.deinit (here 50,000 tokens, 18,623 distinct, about 37% first occurrences per pass).
Memory-tight jobs: Zig peaked at 4.2 MB RSS on this test against 7.5-7.9 MB for the C++ rows, 5.1-5.5 MB for C, 5.4 MB for Rust and 11.3 MB for Go.
As evidence when reviewing C++ text tooling: a tokenizer built on std::istringstream and std::unordered_map<std::string,int> loses 1.7x even to bounds-checked Zig on this input shape.
when_not_to_use: Inside a C++ codebase: rewrite the C++ with std::string_view tokens and an open-addressing map instead; the suite never measured such a version, so how much of the 1.74x it would recover is unmeasured.
When the source text is freed or modified while the map is alive: the keys are slices into it and would dangle; duplicating keys (allocator.dupe) gives up the zero-copy advantage.
Long-lived or incrementally grown maps: the code never reserves capacity, and an arena does not free the tables discarded on each grow, so memory comes back only at arena.deinit.
Text with tabs, newlines or runs of spaces: splitScalar splits on ' ' only, skips the empty tokens and keeps '\t' or '\n' inside tokens, unlike operator>>, which skips all whitespace.

When you need the fastest production row: Crystal (0.88 s) edges Zig (0.91 s) on the same test; only the unchecked ReleaseFast build (0.57 s) leads clearly, and the suite files that build under 'hack'.

integration.dependencies: none for this task (Zig std: ArenaAllocator, StringHashMap, mem.splitScalar); the suite's build.zig links libc and pcre2-8 and pulls the csv-zero package for other tests
integration.min_toolchain: Zig 0.16 std APIs (the harness uses std.process.Init and std.Io); measured with Zig 0.16.0 (July to September 2026 runs) and 0.17.0 (2026-10-05)
integration.platforms: Measured on x86-64 Linux (AMD Ryzen 7 3800X) built for the host CPU (b.standardTargetOptions default); nothing platform-specific in words.zig
integration.thread_safety: Not documented; the std.HashMap source read has no locking (only a safe-mode pointer-stability assertion), and the benchmark is single-threaded

gotchas: Harness flaw against the suite's own rules: the author's first rule (issue #1) is 'Try to use the same semantics, same constructs and containers - this is most important', and the Crystal reference (crystal/main.cr) builds a fresh String per word with String#split, yet the Zig port keys its map with zero-copy slices inside an arena while C++ copies every new key into a heap node. Much of the 1.74x is that implementation choice, not Zig.

Checksums reproduce: a Python replay of the suite's LCG gives a 325,090-byte text with 18,623 distinct words and a unique top word ('tea', 9 times), and reaches run.js's 1998586832 only as 432 runs (72 untimed warm-up plus 360 timed). Zig keeps the first maximum in hash-iteration order, so a tied top count would make the checksum order-dependent; this input has no tie.

The C++ generator computes Helper::next_int(word_len) + Helper::next_int(3) + 3, whose operand evaluation order C++ leaves unspecified (Zig and C sequence the two calls left to right); a compiler that evaluated right to left would build a different text and fail the checksum rather than skew timing. The results file does not record checksum status.

One timing per configuration per monthly run, no variance; the README itself says its ranking reflects 50 tasks, 'not my pick for a single test'. Code and lead were stable: zig/src/words.zig is unchanged since 2026-02-28 and cpp/src/words.cpp since 2026-04-24, and Zig led the best C/C++ row by 1.712x, 1.725x, 1.716x, 1.708x and 1.744x from 2026-07-14 to 2026-10-05 (derived from the results files).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Among the catalogued Etc::Words rows, Zig has the lowest peak RSS (4.2 MB against Crystal 8.8, Rust 5.4 and Go 11.3) and the fastest unchecked build (0.57 s), while Crystal's production row is marginally faster (0.88 vs 0.91 s) and Rust (1.021 s) and Go (1.129 s) trail; pick the Zig pattern when you want explicit control of key lifetime and allocation. For production text tools, the catalogued CLI siblings (huniq, cuniq, runiq) are real programs; this row is only a code pattern.
verified_claims_summary: On an AMD Ryzen 7 3800X (results 2026-10-05), the Zig 0.17.0 ReleaseSafe build ran 360 timed iterations in 0.91 s against 1.587 s for the best of the 16 GCC 16.0.1 and Clang 22.1.8 C and C++ builds (C++/G++/PGO; libstdc++ istringstream plus unordered_map), 1.638 s for the -O2 prod C++/G++ row and 1.96-2.0 s for the C uthash rows: about 1.74x, derived from page data. The four earlier monthly runs (Zig 0.16.0) give 1.71-1.73x.
status_note: Active MIT-licensed suite (41 stars, last commit 2026-10-08, monthly reruns) and words.zig is a copyable 130-line pattern, but no timing bug was found: the C, C++ and Zig harnesses time run_all the same way after a 20% untimed warm-up and verify the checksum; the flaw is that the Zig port uses zero-copy keys and an arena that the Crystal reference and the suite's 'same containers' rule do not, so read the row as 'the C++ idiom is slow', not 'Zig codegen beats C++'.
